whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Identity and Access Management Architect exam for?

personas.label: Identity architects
personas.description: You design how people and systems log in, and you want the credential that proves it.

personas.label: Integration specialists
personas.description: You build server-to-server connections and need to pick the right OAuth flow with confidence.

personas.label: Security engineers
personas.description: You own multi-factor authentication, Connected Apps and session policy for a Salesforce org.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Identity and Access Management Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: It is a demanding exam because the answers turn on small differences between protocols. You need to know SAML and the OAuth flows well enough to match one to a specific situation, not just describe them. It is one of the four exams that earn the System Architect credential.
bullets: About 58% to pass, roughly 35 correct answers out of 60. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book.
Protocol detail matters. Expect questions where two OAuth flows both look workable and only one fits.
Single sign-on design. Know which side starts the login, how users are provisioned, and what Salesforce can do as an identity provider.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can sketch each OAuth flow from memory, set up SAML single sign-on in both directions, and say what a Connected App's scopes and policies control. Aim for 75% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Identity and Access Management Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a login or integration situation and ask which flow, setting or feature fits. The detail that decides it is usually whether a person is involved and whether the app can hold a secret safely.
bestWayToPass: Match each OAuth flow to its situation: Web server when a person logs in through a browser, JWT bearer for server-to-server with no user, device flow for a TV or CLI, user-agent for a browser or mobile app.
Set up SAML both ways: Salesforce as the service provider logging users in from an outside provider, and Salesforce as the identity provider for other apps.
Learn Connected App controls: Scopes, IP restrictions, session policies and which users are pre-authorised.
Know the multi-factor rules: What satisfies the requirement, and how single sign-on interacts with it.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests how you design login and access for Salesforce: single sign-on with SAML, the OAuth flows, Connected Apps, multi-factor authentication, and how user accounts are created and kept in step.

keyConcepts.h2: Identity and Access Management Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Authentication and Authorisation Are Not the Same
blocks.body: **Authentication** proves who someone is, which is logging in. **Authorisation** decides what they may then do or which data an app may reach. SAML handles authentication for people. OAuth handles authorisation for applications: it gives an app a token to act on someone's behalf, or on its own behalf, without handing over a password. OpenID Connect sits on top of OAuth and adds an identity token, so an app learns who the user is as well as what it may do. Many exam questions become easy once you decide which of the two the scenario is really about.

blocks.heading: SAML Single Sign-On: Who Starts the Login
blocks.body: With **SAML**, the **identity provider** checks the user and vouches for them, and the **service provider** is the app they are reaching. In **service-provider-initiated** single sign-on the user starts at Salesforce, is redirected to the provider to log in, and comes back with an assertion. In **identity-provider-initiated** single sign-on the user starts at the provider's portal and clicks through to Salesforce. Setup needs the provider's certificate, the entity ID and the login URL to match on both sides, and Salesforce needs **My Domain** turned on. Typical failures are a mismatched entity ID, an expired certificate, or clocks out of step so the assertion looks stale. Salesforce can also be the identity provider for other applications.

blocks.heading: OAuth 2.0 Flows and When Each Fits
blocks.body: **Web server flow** (authorisation code) is for apps with a server that can keep a secret, where a person logs in through a browser. **User-agent flow** suits apps running in a browser or on a phone, where no secret can be hidden. **JWT bearer flow** is for server-to-server access with no person present: the app signs an assertion with a certificate and receives a token. **Client credentials flow** also covers server-to-server work tied to a single integration user. **Device flow** is for devices with awkward input, such as a TV, where the user authorises on another screen. **Refresh tokens** let an app get new access tokens without asking the user again, and their lifetime is controlled by policy.

blocks.heading: Connected Apps: Scopes, Policies and Sessions
blocks.body: A **Connected App** is how an outside application is registered with Salesforce. Its **scopes** limit what a token may do, for example reading data, managing the user's account or acting offline with a refresh token. **Policies** control who may use it: admin pre-authorised; so only chosen profiles or permission sets can connect, or self-authorised, where any user may approve it. You can restrict it to trusted **IP ranges**, set how long sessions last, and set a refresh token policy such as expiring after a period of inactivity. Newer orgs may use External Client Apps for the same purpose. Revoking the app's tokens cuts off access immediately.

blocks.heading: Provisioning, Multi-Factor and My Domain
blocks.body: Accounts have to be created and removed as well as authenticated. **Just-in-time provisioning** creates or updates a Salesforce user from the SAML assertion the first time they log in. **User provisioning** for Connected Apps pushes accounts out to other systems. **SCIM** is the standard many identity providers use for the same job. **Multi-factor authentication** is required for Salesforce access, and the requirement can be met by a verification method in Salesforce or by single sign-on where the provider enforces it. **My Domain** gives the org its own login URL, which single sign-on and several identity features depend on. For customers, Experience Cloud supports social sign-on and self-registration.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Identity and Access Management Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Nearly every question is a choice between protocols or flows. Look for whether a person is present, whether a secret can be kept, and which side starts the login.

blocks.heading: Choosing an OAuth Flow
blocks.body: Person plus a server that keeps a secret: web server flow. No person at all: JWT bearer. Browser or mobile app with no secret: user-agent. Limited input device: device flow.

blocks.heading: SAML Setup and Failures
blocks.body: Entity ID, certificate and login URL must match on both sides, and My Domain must be on. Mismatched IDs, expired certificates and clock drift are the usual causes of failure.

blocks.heading: Connected App Controls
blocks.body: Scopes limit what a token can do. Admin pre-authorisation limits who can connect. IP ranges and session policies tighten it further.

blocks.heading: Multi-Factor Authentication
blocks.body: The requirement can be satisfied inside Salesforce or by the identity provider through single sign-on. Know which methods count.

blocks.heading: Provisioning Users
blocks.body: Just-in-time provisioning creates users during single sign-on. SCIM and user provisioning keep accounts in step and remove leavers.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: This is one of the four exams for System Architect. Good next steps:

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary focus of an Identity and Access Management Architect?
options: Designing solutions that meet Single Sign-On (SSO) and identity requirements on the Salesforce Platform
sampleQuestions.explanation: They design solutions that meet SSO and identity requirements on the platform.
whyWrong: Email is unrelated to the IAM Architect's core identity/SSO focus.
'Only reports' undersells the role, which is about SSO and identity architecture, not reporting.
Slack is unrelated to the IAM Architect's core identity/SSO focus.

sampleQuestions.question: Which protocol is commonly used for SSO with Salesforce?
sampleQuestions.explanation: SAML 2.0 and OAuth 2.0 are used for SSO and identity with Salesforce.
whyWrong: 'Only SOAP' is an API messaging protocol, not the specific SSO protocols being asked about.
'Only HTTP' is a generic transport protocol, not the specific identity protocols (SAML/OAuth) used for SSO.
'Only FTP' is a file transfer protocol, unrelated to SSO.

sampleQuestions.question: What does My Domain provide in Salesforce?
options: Custom login URL and foundation for SSO and identity
sampleQuestions.explanation: My Domain provides custom login URL and is required for SSO and identity features.
whyWrong: 'Only reports' is unrelated to My Domain's actual identity/URL foundation purpose.
'Only branding' undersells My Domain, which specifically establishes the SSO/identity foundation, not just visual branding.
'Only dashboards' is unrelated to My Domain's actual identity/URL foundation purpose.

sampleQuestions.question: Which feature allows users to log in once and access multiple connected apps?
sampleQuestions.explanation: SSO allows one login to access multiple connected applications.
whyWrong: 'Only roles' misattributes single-login access to a different access-control feature.
'Only profiles' misattributes single-login access to a different access-control feature.
'Only permission sets' misattributes single-login access to a different access-control feature.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Connected Apps in identity?
options: OAuth-based access for external and internal apps with configurable policies
sampleQuestions.explanation: Connected Apps provide OAuth-based access with configurable policies.
whyWrong: 'Only internal apps' undersells Connected Apps, which manage both external and internal app access.
'Only email' is unrelated to Connected Apps' OAuth-based access purpose.
'Only external apps' undersells Connected Apps, which manage both external and internal app access.

sampleQuestions.question: What is an Identity Provider (IdP) in SSO?
options: The system that authenticates users and asserts identity to Salesforce
sampleQuestions.explanation: IdP authenticates users and asserts identity to Salesforce.
whyWrong: A permission set controls object/field access, it isn't an authentication system.
A profile controls access levels, it isn't an authentication/identity-asserting system.
Salesforce alone isn't the IdP in this scenario, the IdP is the external system asserting identity.

sampleQuestions.question: Which OAuth flow is used for server-to-server integration?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Client credentials and JWT bearer are for server-to-server.
whyWrong: Authorization code flow is designed for user-facing scenarios, not server-to-server integration.
Implicit flow is a simplified user-facing flow, not designed for secure server-to-server integration.
Device flow is for devices without browsers, not the typical server-to-server integration scenario.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Session Security Level control?
options: Session requirements (e.g., high assurance, require re-auth)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Session Security Level enforces session assurance requirements.
whyWrong: 'Only timeout' undersells Session Security Level, which covers broader session requirements beyond just timeout.
'Only OWD' misattributes session security to an unrelated record-access concept.
'Only IP' undersells Session Security Level, which is about broader assurance/re-auth requirements, not just IP restriction.

sampleQuestions.question: Which SAML attribute is used for user provisioning?
options: Federation ID and other attributes for matching/provisioning
sampleQuestions.explanation: Federation ID and attributes support user matching and provisioning.
whyWrong: 'Only email' undersells the Federation ID's specific matching/provisioning role.
'Only role' undersells the Federation ID's specific matching/provisioning role.
'Only name' undersells the Federation ID, which serves the specific matching/provisioning purpose described.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Auth. Provider?
options: To configure external IdP connection (e.g., SAML, OAuth)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Auth. Provider configures external IdP (SAML/OAuth) connection.
whyWrong: 'To create users only' undersells Auth. Provider's broader identity connection purpose.
Auth. Provider doesn't replace SSO, it configures the external connection SSO relies on.
'To assign permission sets' is unrelated to what an Auth. Provider configures.

sampleQuestions.question: Which feature supports multi-factor authentication?
sampleQuestions.explanation: 2FA and verified modes support multi-factor authentication.
whyWrong: 'SSO only' misattributes multi-factor authentication to a different, single-login feature.
'OAuth only' misattributes MFA to a different authorization protocol.
'SAML only' misattributes MFA to a different SSO protocol.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Federation ID enable?
options: Linking Salesforce user to external identity for SSO and provisioning
sampleQuestions.explanation: Federation ID links Salesforce user to external identity.
whyWrong: 'Only SSO' undersells Federation ID's specific role in both SSO and provisioning.
'Only permission sets' is unrelated to Federation ID's actual identity-linking purpose.
'Only OAuth' misattributes Federation ID's purpose to a different protocol.

sampleQuestions.question: Which consideration applies when designing for multiple IdPs?
options: Domain-based routing and IdP selection logic
whyWrong: 'Single IdP only' is the opposite of the multi-IdP scenario the question describes.
'Manual only' contradicts the fact that automated routing logic is the actual design consideration.
'No routing' contradicts the fact that domain-based routing is a real design consideration for multiple IdPs.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Certificate and Key Management?
options: To manage SAML certificates and signing keys for trust
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certificate management ensures SAML and signing key trust.
whyWrong: 'To create users' misattributes certificate/key management's actual trust-and-signing purpose.
'To assign profiles' is unrelated to certificate and key management.
'To create permission sets' is unrelated to certificate and key management.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best practice supports identity governance?
options: Regular access reviews, least privilege, and audit logging
sampleQuestions.explanation: Access reviews, least privilege, and audit support governance.
whyWrong: 'No review' contradicts the fact that regular access reviews are a core identity governance best practice.
'No logging' contradicts the fact that audit logging is a core identity governance best practice.
'All access' contradicts the least-privilege principle that's central to good identity governance.

expertInsight: This exam rewards precision. Several OAuth flows can technically move a token around; but only one fits the situation described, and the deciding detail is usually whether a person is present and whether the app can keep a secret. Learn to spot those two things in the question. The other area worth drilling is SAML: know which side starts the login, and what breaks when the clock or the entity ID is wrong.
